strengths: The input-sensitivity objective is an interesting empirical approach to unlearning. Operating without retained data or stored training trajectories addresses a useful practical constraint.

Full-class removal shows promising utility preservation: on CIFAR-100, MU-Mis reaches 0% forget accuracy while retaining 76.32% accuracy, compared with 76.36% before unlearning. Results on the face dataset are also competitive with retraining.

The loss ablation provides concrete evidence that combining the two terms improves utility: retained accuracy is 76.32%, versus 60.45% when suppressing target-class sensitivity alone. The experiments include several established baselines, three deletion settings, and runtime comparisons.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification in Section 3.2 is unsound as written. Differentiating the training updates omits derivatives of the loss gradient and the dependence of intermediate weights on training data, without controlling these omissions. Furthermore, g_k g'_kᵀ is not generally symmetric, so the asserted equality between contribution and sensitivity terms is unjustified for multiclass outputs. The assumption that the sum of cross-sample terms is negligible also lacks a bound or direct validation. Consequently, the claimed connection to sample-deletion influence is not established.

The privacy evaluation is insufficiently diagnostic. MIA reports only the fraction of forgotten examples classified as members, without false-positive rates, adequate attack specifications, or stronger attack comparisons. Retrained models receive 94% and 95.4% in Tables 5 and 4. These numbers do not themselves establish leakage; they demonstrate why treating a lower membership-prediction rate as stronger unlearning is unreliable. Accuracy and attention-map changes cannot independently establish removal of training information.

The random-subset experiment provides little evidence beyond leaving the model unchanged. In Table 5, pretrained and MU-Mis models both have 94.67% retain accuracy and 100% forget accuracy; MIA changes only from 95% to 94% on 100 examples. Retraining already produces nearly identical aggregate metrics. More discriminating experiments and per-example comparisons against retrained models are needed to support individual-sample unlearning.

Claims of consistent, significant superiority exceed the experimental evidence. Evaluation uses only ResNet18, a few selected classes, and one random-subset size, without repeated-run uncertainty. Several improvements are small, including 0.26 percentage points over SSD in Table 1 and 0.10 over Blindspot in Table 3. Ablations cover only full-class deletion and do not establish robustness to stopping thresholds, deletion sizes, or the choice of non-target classes.

Reproducibility is materially incomplete. Numerical stopping thresholds and their selection procedure are missing, baseline configurations are sparse, and code is only promised. Algorithm 1 never updates its accumulated loss and places the stopping check outside the purported maximum-iteration loop. Additionally, the motivation sums unsquared norms over non-target classes, whereas the implemented objective uses squared norms and a sampled class; the resulting change in weighting is neither explained nor ablated.
